questions.stem: Gabby, 41, lies still in the ED with constant right upper quadrant pain, fever and vomiting. Examining her abdomen, you tell the examiner you will now check for Murphy's sign. Which manoeuvre correctly elicits it?
options: Ask her to lift her head off the trolley while you press on the tender area
Flex and internally rotate her right hip while watching her face for pain
Rest fingers under the right costal margin, midclavicular line, and ask her to breathe in
Press deeply over the tender point, then release suddenly and watch her face
questions.why: On deep inspiration the diaphragm pushes the inflamed gallbladder down onto the examiner's fingers, so she catches her breath and stops inhaling. It is positive only if the same manoeuvre on the left does not hurt.
notes: This is Carnett's sign. It helps tell abdominal wall pain from visceral pain but does not test the gallbladder.
This is the obturator sign, used for a pelvic appendix or a pelvic abscess irritating obturator internus, not the gallbladder.
This tests for rebound tenderness, a sign of peritonism. It is not specific to the gallbladder and is unkind to a patient already in severe pain.

questions.stem: Gabby, 41, has acute calculous cholecystitis on ultrasound (TG18 grade I). T 38.8 °C, HR 114, BP 122/74, WCC 15.8, normal renal function, no drug allergies. She is vomiting. Blood cultures have just been taken. Which antibiotic plan matches eTG?
options: Amoxicillin 2 g IV 6-hourly plus gentamicin IV, single daily dose by weight
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg oral 12-hourly and discharge to surgical clinic
Meropenem 1 g IV 8-hourly until blood culture results are available
Withhold antibiotics until blood cultures identify an organism
questions.why: eTG recommends IV amoxicillin 2 g 6-hourly plus gentamicin (4 to 7 mg/kg, dosing interval by renal function) for acute cholecystitis, with ceftriaxone 2 g IV daily if gentamicin is contraindicated. She is admitted for early laparoscopic cholecystectomy.
notes: She is febrile, tachycardic and vomiting. She needs IV therapy and admission for early cholecystectomy, not oral antibiotics at home.
Meropenem is held back for resistant organisms such as ESBL producers. Using it first line for mild community-acquired biliary sepsis is poor stewardship.
She has fever, tachycardia and a high WCC. Antibiotics start straight after blood cultures and are not delayed for culture results.

questions.stem: Gabby, 41, says her pain began within an hour of a large creamy pasta dinner, and her earlier shorter episodes also came after rich meals. Which hormone, released when fat reaches the duodenum, makes her gallbladder contract against the stone impacted in its neck?
options: Gastrin from gastric antral G cells
questions.why: Fatty acids and amino acids in the duodenum release cholecystokinin from I cells. It contracts the gallbladder and relaxes the sphincter of Oddi. Contraction against a blocked cystic duct raises the pressure in the gallbladder and causes pain after meals.
notes: Secretin is released mainly in response to acid. It drives bicarbonate secretion from the pancreatic ducts and has little effect on gallbladder contraction.
Gastrin drives gastric acid secretion and antral motility. It is not the main hormone that makes the gallbladder contract after a fatty meal.
Somatostatin inhibits gallbladder contraction and the secretion of most GI hormones, so it does the opposite of what is asked.

questions.stem: Gabby, 41, has acute cholecystitis. Her constant right upper quadrant pain now goes up into the tip of her right shoulder. The inflamed gallbladder is irritating the peritoneum on the central undersurface of the diaphragm. Which nerve carries this pain and explains the referral?
questions.why: The phrenic nerve (C3 to C5) carries sensation from the central diaphragm and its peritoneum. The supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4) share these segments and supply the skin over the shoulder tip, so the pain is felt there.
notes: The splanchnic nerves carry visceral pain from the gallbladder itself, felt as poorly localised epigastric or RUQ pain, not shoulder tip pain.
These supply the peripheral diaphragm and the parietal peritoneum of the abdominal wall. They cause local pain at the costal margin and abdominal wall, not shoulder pain.
The vagus carries parasympathetic and visceral reflex fibres, for example for nausea. It does not carry somatic diaphragmatic pain to the C3 to C5 segments.
